newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST- US Q4 ECI may hint at broader price rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- US Q4 ECI may hint at broader price rise.

text.p: With continuing labor shortages forcing U.S. employers to shell out higher wages to attract qualified workers, analysts said they see a troubling rise in general price inflation lurking just around the corner.
One of the most reliable gauges of wage growth, the quarterly report on the Employment Cost Index (ECI), is due next Tuesday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Economists generally expect the index rose by nearly 1.0 percent in the fourth quarter.
That would represent an increase from the more manageable 0.6-percent gain in the third quarter, and a sure sign overall inflation will soon rise, analysts said.

"Historically, increases in labor compensation have been a leading indicator of higher core inflation. Things aren't going to the moon, but it seems to me really a question of time before we see the core going up," said Paul Kasriel, chief domestic economist at Northern Trust.
Recent monthly data show average hourly earnings trending higher in November and December, suggesting the quarterly ECI data will rise sharply as well.
The Labor Department reported average hourly earnings rose nearly 0.8 percent in November and 0.5 percent in December.
"With those data, you have to expect an increase baked in the cake (on ECI). We're getting to the point where we do have to worry about it," said Salomon Brothers economist Brian Jones.

With the economy currently operating at or past its optimal level by many traditional measures, signs of faster wage growth will likely nudge Federal Reserve policy makers toward a hike in short-term interest rates, analysts said.
"It may not even take a deterioration in actual inflation numbers for the Fed to move," said Jones. "At these high employment levels, we don't need to see tremendous growth for the Fed to go.

The central bank has held the overnight federal funds rate target at 5.25 percent for almost a year despite a U.S. jobless rate that has held below 6.0 percent since late 1994 and stood at 5.3 percent in December.
Many economists believe unemployment at the current level will eventually foster higher inflation.

"We are running into capacity constraints in terms of human capital. In this environment, some businesses can raise prices. They can't raise their output because they have to pay more for labor," Kasriel said.

But by some combination of lower profit margins, unseen productivity gains and better control of nonwage costs, U.S. firms have been able to eat higher wages without passing them on to final goods prices, analysts said.
"There is a lot of room between wage increases and price increases," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp.
"We are in a tolerable zone, both for the economy and maybe from the Fed's point-of-view, if the consumer price index (CPI) stays near 3.0 percent," Hoffman said.

Only one of 29 economists polled by Reuters expected the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee to hike official interest rates when it meets February 4-5. But many forecast a rate hike by the end of the first half.

Over the last six years, CPI has held at or below 3.0 percent despite a continuous U.S. economic expansion. But economists said that trend may end in 1997, with CPI edging up by a quarter- or half-percentage point.
"We will see a drift up, which will create some anxiety at the Fed. But it won't be a radical jump in inflation," Kasriel said.
